idiom_name: asyncio.gather(*(route(p) for p in parts)) + reduce
implementation_notes: asyncio.gather schedules one task per part and returns the results in the order of the awaitables regardless of completion order - that list is the aggregation input and its index is the correlation state; TaskGroup (3.11+) is the structured variant that cancels the remaining tasks when one raises. The classic Aggregator object is only needed once parts leave the process (a broker, a worker fleet); in-process, gather plus a reduce is the complete realization.
code_sketch:
async def process(order: dict) -> Report:
    parts = split(order)                                  # [{kind, payload}, ...]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(route(p) for p in parts))
    return functools.reduce(lambda acc, r: acc.merge(r), results, Report.empty())
pitfalls: gather() (unlike TaskGroup) does not cancel the remaining tasks when one raises, so losing parts keep running and may fail later unnoticed.
A blocking call inside route() blocks the event loop and serialises the fan-out; offload with asyncio.to_thread or a ProcessPoolExecutor.
Unbounded gather over a large parts list creates thousands of tasks; gate with an asyncio.Semaphore or chunk the parts.

variants.name: Celery chord (header group + body callback)
variants.idiom_name: celery.chord(group(route.s(p) for p in parts), merge.s())
variants.implementation_notes: Celery's chord is the distributed realization: the canvas chapter defines a chord as a group with a callback, so group(route.s(p) for p in parts) is the split and fan-out, the body task merge.s() is the aggregator, and the broker plus result backend hold the correlation state across process restarts. Chunks (chord of chunks) bound the fan-out when the part count is large, and each part can be retried independently - the reasons to accept the broker dependency in exchange for horizontal scale.
pitfalls: The chord body runs only when every header task succeeded and the results could be stored: a lost or failed part leaves the composite without an aggregate unless the body is also scheduled on failure (link_error/chord_errback).
Chords need a result backend to hand the header results to the body; without one the callback cannot fire (the canvas chapter notes chords are a group with a callback receiving the results).
Free prefetched parts and worker restarts can redeliver header tasks, so route() must be idempotent or the aggregate double-counts.
